header:
Date: 2025-09-30
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 mins
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (NexaVue Head of ML), Aisha Khan (Platform Engineer), Tom Reed (CTO)
summary: POC scoping call to size capacity and autoscale strategy for NexaVue's LLM-powered features. Discussed reserved GPU baseline, burst strategy for traffic peaks, fallback policies to cheaper model variants or hosted routes, success criteria (latency p95 < 250ms, throughput 400rps sustained, cost target), benchmark plan and timeline. Agreed next steps: send pricing, run benchmarks with sample workload, provision trial dedicated cluster for 2 weeks.
transcript:
00:00 Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, on time. This is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE on this. We've got Priya from our SE team and I think NexaVue folks on, could you quick intros?
00:08 Carlos Mendes: Yeah, Carlos here, head of ML at NexaVue. We own the recommendation engine, we want to add a chat assistant for ops and customer messages.
00:13 Aisha Khan: Aisha, platform eng, I'll be working on infra side of the POC.
00:16 Tom Reed: Tom, CTO, high-level observer.
00:20 Priya Raman: Hi all — Priya, Redwood SE, I'll lead the benchmark and capacity scoping.
00:24 Jordan Lee: Great. Quick agenda: success criteria, current workload and QPS, reserved baseline sizing, burst strategy, fallbacks, and timeline. Sound good?
00:31 Carlos Mendes: Yep. To give context, our current traffic for the feature will be a mix: internal ops chat ~50 qps peak, and external customer-facing chat expected to ramp to 300–500 qps during promos. Right now it's all server-side small models. We're looking at latency p95 under 250ms for the customer chat, and cost needs to be within X% of current infra spend — we'll define exact dollar target later.
00:56 Priya Raman: Got it. Can you confirm average token length per request and tokenization? That affects GPU memory and KV cache sizing.
01:02 Carlos Mendes: Average prompt ~120 tokens, with expected generation ~80 tokens. Some outliers up to 600 tokens for long support threads. Tokenization is standard bpe from the open model variant.
01:14 Priya Raman: Perfect. So for capacity planning we typically size a reserved baseline to cover sustained throughput — e.g., what you expect 95% of the time — and then allow burst capacity for spikes. For the POC we recommend reserving GPUs to cover your steady-state CPU and KV cache needs and enabling burst-on-demand to handle the 99th percentile events.
01:31 Aisha Khan: When you say reserved GPUs, are these per-tenant? How isolated is the data plane? We need VPC peering and KMS integration for keys.
01:39 Jordan Lee: Yes — Dedicated reserved pools are customer-isolated, VPC peering supported, and we integrate with KMS/HSM for key material. We'll share the security pack.
01:47 Tom Reed: Also want to understand fallback policies: if dedicated capacity is saturated, what happens? Do we shift to hosted models or a smaller quantized model?
01:56 Priya Raman: Good question. Typical Redwood approach: policy-driven routing — first try reserved Dedicated GPUs pinned to your model variant; if latency or queue depth breaches thresholds, we route to a compatible, lower-cost variant (quantized or smaller architecture) in the same region, or fall back to hosted endpoints if that's acceptable for you. We can also configure graceful degradation like shorter max tokens or response truncation.
02:15 Carlos Mendes: What's the typical latency hit when falling back to a quantized variant? We care about user experience.
02:19 Priya Raman: For most encoder-decoder style models, INT8 quantization adds minimal latency — maybe 5–15ms extra per token — but you can see slight quality differences. Switching to a smaller architecture can add 20–80ms depending on model. We should include subjective quality checks in the benchmark.
02:35 Jordan Lee: For the POC success criteria let's capture: 1) latency p95 < 250ms for customer chat on 90% of traffic, 2) sustain 400 rps for 10-minute windows, 3) no more than 5% of requests served by fallback with acceptable QA, and 4) cost per 1k requests under agreed target. Any objections?
02:56 Tom Reed: Fine, but we need quantifiable cost target — maybe you can propose reserved vs burst pricing.
03:01 Jordan Lee: We'll send that.
03:03 Priya Raman: Ok, moving to workload sizing. Based on 120+80 tokens average, our perf matrix suggests one A100-class GPU (or equivalent) can handle roughly 120–150 rps for that sequence length with optimized kernels and batching; with smaller quantized models you can push more. For 400 rps sustained, we'd recommend a reserved baseline of 3 GPUs to give headroom and enable efficient KV caching, then allow bursts to add 2–4 extra GPUs depending on concurrency.
03:28 Aisha Khan: Can you explain the math — how do you get to 120 rps per GPU? We're trying to map to our current infra costs.
03:33 Priya Raman: Sure — the number is from our internal benchmarks: sequence length, model FLOPs, and GPU compute lead to per-token throughput. For your 200 token round-trip average, with batching set to 8 and continuous KV cache, we've seen p50 token latency that supports ~130 rps on an A100. We will run a POC benchmark to validate with your actual prompts and beam search settings.
03:50 Carlos Mendes: For long tails with 600 tokens, we assume those will be routed to a different tier?
03:54 Priya Raman: Yes — we recommend routing very long requests to a different pool with larger seq-length profile or to a lower-concurrency node, to avoid evicting caches for short requests. That helps preserve latency for the bulk of traffic.
04:06 Tom Reed: Autoscaling cadence — how fast can you add GPUs? If there's a sudden spike from 200 to 600 qps, will autoscale respond quick enough?
04:14 Priya Raman: Platform autoscaling has two levers: fast burst (warm spare capacity in the same region) which can push capacity in 30–90s, and cold scale (provision new instances) which can take minutes. For customer-facing low-latency needs, we recommend mixing reserved baseline plus warm spare pool configured as burst capacity. Warm spare is slightly more expensive but avoids cold-start delay.
04:33 Aisha Khan: If warm spare is used frequently that will blow the budget — what's the billing model for warm spare?
04:38 Jordan Lee: Warm spare is billed at a lower reservation discount than fully reserved but higher than pure on-demand. We'll include a cost comparison matrix for reserved, warm-spare, and on-demand bursts in the pricing doc.
04:49 Carlos Mendes: How about queueing policies — do you allow priority lanes? We want ops chat to have higher priority than marketing-driven bursts.
04:55 Priya Raman: Yes, we support per-route priority and token-level SLA. You can set priority rules so ops chat routes to the reserved pool first and customer chat uses reserved + burst. We also support request throttling and graceful backpressure.
05:07 Tom Reed: For the POC timeline, what's realistic? We want results within two weeks.
05:12 Jordan Lee: Typical POC flow: Week 1 — onboarding, security review, share sample dataset, baseline benchmarks; Week 2 — run load tests, tune autoscaling and routing, qualitative evals and final report. We can compress if NexaVue provides sample requests immediately. We're proposing a 2-week trial Dedicated cluster starting 2025-10-06.
05:28 Aisha Khan: Ops will need a network diagram and SSO/SAML details. We'll also want to run a security scan.
05:33 Jordan Lee: Noted. We'll share SOC2, network diagram, and a short guide for VPC peering.
05:38 Carlos Mendes: Benchmarks — we want p95, p99, cost per 1k, and quality regression checks using a 200-sample eval set.
05:46 Priya Raman: We'll set up the benchmark harness to produce p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, and cost numbers. Also include a small human-in-the-loop quality check for the 200 samples. We'll upload the harness and script so you can reproduce.
05:58 Tom Reed: If results are positive, what's next?
06:01 Jordan Lee: Next steps: convert to reserved monthly commit for Dedicated, negotiate SLA and volume discounts. We'll capture that in the pricing doc.
06:06 Carlos Mendes: Sounds good. A couple of quick clarifying questions: 1) can you pin a model version during POC? 2) can we limit data retention?
06:13 Priya Raman: Yes to both — model pinning supported, and data retention/TTL configurable on Dedicated; we can route logs to your S3 and respect retention policies.
06:20 Aisha Khan: One more — fallback visibility. We need to log when a request was served by fallback and why.
06:25 Priya Raman: We'll surface fallback reasons in the trace and in the Console with per-request tags.
06:30 Jordan Lee: Okay, summarizing next steps: Jordan to send pricing and reserved vs burst comparison, Priya to prepare benchmark harness and schedule the first run on 2025-10-03, NexaVue to provide sample workload (10k requests) and infra contacts by 2025-10-01, and Redwood to provision a 2-week Dedicated trial starting 2025-10-06 pending security sign-off.
06:49 Carlos Mendes: That timeline works for us.
06:51 Tom Reed: Thanks — looking forward to the benchmark.
06:54 Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email and attach the security pack. Bye.
06:58 (call ends)
